overview.text: In mathematics, infinity describes what has no finite bound or end; the symbol ∞ is not an ordinary counting number. The idea appears in different ways: a sequence can grow without bound, a limit can increase without bound, and a set can contain infinitely many elements. Set theory compares the sizes of sets by asking whether their elements can be paired one-to-one. This reveals that the natural numbers, integers, and rational numbers share one countable size, ℵ₀, while the real numbers form a larger, uncountable set. Georg Cantor’s work made comparing infinite collections precise and showed that infinity is not just one size.

key_facts.text: A set is countably infinite if its elements can be matched one-to-one with the natural numbers; ℵ₀ names this cardinality.
Although the integers and rational numbers may seem more numerous than the natural numbers, each can be listed in a way that pairs its elements one-to-one with them.
Cantor’s diagonal argument shows that the real numbers cannot all be placed in a one-to-one list with the natural numbers, so their cardinality is larger than ℵ₀.
Cantor proved the real numbers were uncountable in work published in 1874, helping establish the mathematical study of different sizes of infinity.
In modern set theory, there is no largest cardinality: for any set, the set of all its subsets has a strictly larger cardinality.
